connector: It’s Anne Shirley, Anne spelled with an e, and I can hardly breathe for excitement. The Sunday school picnic is nearly here, with boats on the lake and ice cream, which I have never once tasted in my life. Marilla is baking me a basket. Looking forward to it is half the pleasure, and I have been doing a great deal of it. Come along and help me wait.

a.raw: marilla looked in the drawer the closet and the shelf for the brooch
a.fixed: Marilla looked in the drawer, the closet, and the shelf for the brooch.
a.why: A capital M on the name Marilla, commas between the items in the list, and a period at the end.

b.raw: marilla packed bread cookies and a pie into the basket
b.fixed: Marilla packed bread, cookies, and a pie into the basket.
b.why: The same pattern: a capital on the name Marilla, commas between the three items in the list, and a period at the end.

scholar.journal-q1: … and say what made Marilla so sure, when Anne had never told her a story before.
scholar.journal-q2: … then say what Anne got wrong about what a confession is for.
scholar.journal-q3: … and say what Marilla admits at the end, and what it cost her to admit it.

fill1.h1: Above your head. Which part means above?
fill1.why: over- means above: overhead is above your head.

fill2.h1: Too much sleep. Which part can also mean too much?
fill2.why: over- can mean too much: to oversleep is to sleep too long.

fill3.h1: A line drawn beneath a word. This one is the plain English word for beneath.
fill3.why: under- means below: to underline is to draw a line under.

fill4.h1: A train that runs below the street. Which review part is the short one from Latin?
fill4.why: sub- means under: a subway runs under the ground.

vfill1.h1: What kind of mouth shows a person has made up her mind? Look for the word with resolve inside it.
vfill1.why: resolute: firm and determined. Mrs. Barry’s mouth showed she was not easily moved.

vfill2.h1: How did Diana feel when she heard a name she loved? Look for the word with rapt inside it.
vfill2.why: enraptured: carried away with delight. Diana loved the name Idlewild.

vfill3.h1: Somebody who wants to pay back every hurt. Which word means full of revenge?
vfill3.why: vindictive: wanting to get back at someone.

g4w9ff1.h1: Two people swearing to be bosom friends. What is it they now have between them?
g4w9ff1.why: friendship is the bond two friends share. You can see the vow; you cannot hold the friendship.

g4w9ff2.h1: Before Green Gables nobody stayed. What is the feeling of being all by yourself?
g4w9ff2.why: loneliness is the feeling of having nobody. It is real, but nobody can photograph it.

g4w9ff3.h1: Saying sorry to somebody who frightens you takes what? Think of a brave heart.
g4w9ff3.why: courage is what it takes to do a hard thing anyway.

g4w9ff4.h1: Nine girls had the sleeves Anne wanted. What is the feeling of minding that? It is green, people say.
g4w9ff4.why: jealousy is wanting what somebody else has, and minding that they have it.

s4w9ff1.h1: LESS-un. The mumbled syllable is spelled with a round letter here.
s4w9ff1.why: lesson: the schwa in the second syllable is spelled o.

s4w9ff2.h1: GAR-dun. Your ear says u, but there is no u in it. Picture the word on a seed packet.
s4w9ff2.why: garden: the schwa in the second syllable is spelled e.

s4w9ff3.h1: uh-BOUT. The mumbled syllable is the first one, and it is one letter long.
s4w9ff3.why: about: the schwa in the first syllable is spelled a.

s4w9ff4.h1: RIB-un. Same letter as lesson. Picture the word on a spool.
s4w9ff4.why: ribbon: the schwa in the second syllable is spelled o.

transcripts.welcome: Hello, it’s Anne Shirley, and I’m guiding you again, which is a great honour. Today’s question is how one bad choice grows into a bigger trouble, and you’re to follow the chain link by link. I know something about that, though I’d rather not say what yet. In word study you build the answers yourself instead of sorting them. And the reading move isn’t in the warm-up today. It’s waiting on the Reading tab.
transcripts.dol: The model has a list in it, and I adore lists. Look at what separates the things in the list, and at the little word before the last one. The sentence you’re fixing has three places and one person’s name. Write it out first, then put in what’s missing, one thing at a time. Read it aloud. If you run out of breath in the wrong spot, something is still missing.
transcripts.guide1: Word study! Today you produce the answers yourself, so there’s nowhere to hide, which I find rather thrilling and slightly alarming. Four word parts to type, three of this week’s words to fit into sentences, four feeling words, and four single letters. In every game, read the whole sentence before you type into its gap. A gap on its own will fool you every time. Check each box before you move on.
transcripts.morphology: Read the little description after each word before anything else. It tells you exactly where the part points: above, or too much, or under, or below. Then choose. If two parts seem to fit, say the whole word aloud both ways and trust your ear, because you’ve heard these words before, even if you didn’t know it. If you miss one, a line will tell you why. Read it, then try again.
transcripts.vocabulary: Four words in the bank and only three gaps, so one gets left out, poor thing. Read each sentence to the end. Then ask what job the gap is doing. Is it describing a mouth, a feeling, or a temper? That narrows it wonderfully. Try your word in the sentence out loud. If it sounds foolish, it is. Leave the hardest gap for last and the bank will have done half your work.
transcripts.grammar: Every answer is in the bank, and every one names a feeling or an idea, not a thing you could hold. I have a great many. Read the whole sentence and ask what the person is feeling, or what two people have between them. Then find the bank word for it. When you’ve finished, combine the two short sentences in the box. Put the feeling in as a noun. Don’t just glue them with and.
transcripts.spelling: Two decisions each time. First, say the word and find the syllable that gets mumbled. The description tells you which one. Second, decide which letter is doing the mumbling. Your ear can’t tell you that. The sound is the same for all three letters, which I think is very unfair. So picture the word the way you’ve seen it in a book. If you’ve never seen it, guess, and read the line that comes back.
transcripts.guide2: Two more days till the picnic, and I have thought of very little else, which Marilla says is setting my heart on things. This week’s watch is about finding out what you’ll trade to get what you want. I want that picnic more than anything. As you read, keep two lists in your head: what somebody wants, and what they give up for it. Then decide whether the trade was worth it.
transcripts.wgrd: Careful, now. Next is not the same as because. I get those mixed up when I’m upset. Before you start, get ready to list the order of things as they happen: first, second, third, and nothing else. Then take each pair and say them with because in the middle. If it sounds wrong, it was only next. When you find the real cause, it will be a feeling, not an event. It nearly always is.
transcripts.read: Two stops. The first comes partway through, right after somebody makes a confession, and it asks what that tells you about her and the truth. Don’t decide too quickly. The second is for when you’ve finished, and it asks whether getting what you want by telling somebody what they already believe really counts. Keep your book open beside you. The questions want the chain of events in order.
transcripts.rwm: That sentence is about Marilla, and I only saw the outside of it, which was quite bad enough. The author lets you see the inside. Before you write, read it once and put your hand where that feeling would go in your own body. When you write yours, give the feeling a verb that moves, and send it somewhere: a throat, a stomach, a pair of hands. Don’t name the feeling and stop.
transcripts.guide3: Well, now you know the worst of me. Marilla thought I’d lost her brooch, and I hadn’t, and she shut me in my room until I confessed. So I confessed to something I never did, with a bridge in it. Then she found the brooch on her shawl, and I went to the picnic after all, and the ice cream was sublime. Now say what you noticed, and show it from the book.
transcripts.chapter: The first question asks two things, what I said I did and what Marilla decided I’d done. Keep them apart, because I did keep telling her the truth. The second is about my reasoning, and it made perfect sense at the time. The third wants the chain right to the end, and the last link isn’t the brooch turning up. It’s what Marilla did after. Find it before you answer.
transcripts.wordconn: Your spelling answer is saved, so here’s the connection. All week you’ve been dealing with the vowel you can’t hear, the lazy one that sounds the same however it’s spelled. Your ear can’t tell you which letter it is. You have to look. Well, my confession sounded exactly like the truth. Marilla couldn’t hear the difference either. She had to go and find the brooch to know. When you can’t hear it, look.
transcripts.workshop: Today you map your story: a beginning, three things that go wrong in the middle, and an end. Take my week. I tried on a brooch, and then three things made it worse, each one worse than the last, and it ended with Marilla saying she was wrong and me eating ice cream. Count your middle. One thing is a moment, not a story. Make the third the worst, and make the end change somebody.
